newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Few policy clouds to mar Marshall Plan party.
newsitem.headline: Few policy clouds to mar Marshall Plan party.

text.p: As Europe and the United States prepare to celebrate the 50th anniversary of U.S. aid to post-World War Two Europe on Wednesday, U.S. diplomats say current transatlantic relations are rosier than ever.

Sharp differences on policy towards Cuba and Iran have eased recently, partly from diplomatic efforts and partly circumstance, smoothing the way for U.S. President Bill Clinton's commemorative visit to The Netherlands this week.
The main part of Clinton's Dutch agenda will involve the Marshall Plan, the U.S.-funded programme launched in June 1947 to help rebuild devastated western Europe after World War Two.

Wednesday's European Union-U.S. "summit", slated to last just two hours amid a welter of Marshall Plan ceremony stretching from Tuesday evening to Thursday morning, will touch on foreign policy, transatlantic trade issues and judicial cooperation.

The U.S.-EU talks, headed by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and European Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, will culminate in the signing of two agreements -- on customs and on common controls on trade in chemical ingredients that can be used to make narcotics and chemical weapons.
American officials insisted during advance briefings that EU-U.S. relations had never been better.
They played down possible tensions in The Hague on second-tier issues such as Boeing's planned merger with McDonnell-Douglas Corp or policy differences over veterinary standards or trade in bananas.
Foreign policy discussions were set to range across the global map, from North Korea's nuclear programme, to struggling Middle East peace talks, Bosnia and Africa's Great Lakes region.

Differences have narrowed on Cuba policy, an issue which rankled for months amid EU anger at Washington's Helms-Burton law against third-country firms investing in property taken from U.S. citizens or companies after the 1959 revolution.
Tensions subsided in April with a deal suspending EU protests against Helms-Burton in the World Trade Organisation and staying clauses in the anti-Cuba legislation.
Iran policy, described by one U.S. official last week as "closer than it has been", has also moved to calmer waters.

Washington has long argued for the EU to isolate Iran, which the Americans see as a pariah state that sponsors terrorism, an approach spurned by Germany in particular which has favoured a "critical dialogue" to cajole policy changes out of Tehran.

Policy differences were snatched from diplomats' hands in April, when a Berlin court accused Iran of ordering the 1992 murder of four Kurdish dissidents in Germany, prompting the EU to suspend ministerial meetings with Iran.
Once officials have tackled current business, they will move on to priority issues for the next six months.

These will touch on continued Turkish-Greek Cypriot tensions in divided Cyprus, relations with Turkey, coordination of policy towards China and developments during Hong Kong's transition from British to Chinese rule.

Trade talks will include an update on negotiations for a mutual recognition agreement. The negotiations resumed in Paris on Monday to reach common or equivalent standards for testing and certification of pharmaceuticals and medical equipment.
